text:
OpenClaw vs. Hermes vs. Grok @bot, clearly explained:

All three let you set up an agent with a specific job, and it keeps its files and logins between sessions instead of starting fresh.

OpenClaw and Hermes are self-hosted, so the machine can be a laptop, a VPS, or a container that someone already pays for and can log into.

Grok Bot runs on a machine SpaceXAI provisions and operates. It gives one computer per account rather than one per agent.

Every Bot on that account reads the same files and carries the same browser logins, so handing work between two Bots does not require a re-login or file transfer.

Hermes and OpenClaw isolate agents instead, and their memory sits in plain files anyone can open and edit.

Hermes goes furthest since the agent writes its own skills and a background curator deletes the ones nobody uses.

Grok Bot has the lowest-friction path to a new skill in my opinion.

You can record up to ten minutes of one pass through a workflow, and it can then turn that into a reusable set of instructions and store it as a skill.

Moving on, OpenClaw and Hermes run on any model provider. Grok Bot runs on Grok.

I prepared the graphic below that has the full breakdown, from hosting and memory through to what each of them costs to run.

And if you want to dive deeper, I covered Grok Bot in full in a masterclass, including the shared computer, memory, skills, routines, and the macOS setup.

Read it below.

blocks.text: Everything you need to understand, set up, and get real work out of Grok Bot. It covers what a Bot actually is, how the shared computer works underneath, how it compares to Hermes Agent, and how to run it on yourself.
There is a habit that spread quietly among people running AI agents this year. They leave the laptop lid half open so the agent keeps working. When they close it, the run dies.
That habit belongs to agents that run on your own machine. The hosted ones solved the lid problem long ago, and over the past year they have been solving the memory problem too, in pieces.
For instance:
Devin restores a saved machine snapshot at the start of every session, so anything you did not commit or capture is gone.
Manus puts its sandbox to sleep between tasks and recycles it after enough inactivity, with an always-on cloud computer available.
ChatGPT Work keeps browser cookies, so once you sign in to a site through the takeover flow, later runs pick it up.
Each of those persists one thing, for one agent, usually scoped to a session or a project. You still get a machine per task, and the roster of agents does not share anything.
SpaceXAI launched Grok Bot last week. Instead of a machine per task, you get a machine per person. It stays on, it is tied to your account, and the whole roster of Bots shares it.

This guide covers what a Bot actually is, how the system is put together underneath, how it compares to Hermes Agent and the other options, how to set it up on macOS, and which roles are worth building first.
By the end, you will have a working roster on your own machine, a saved skill, and a routine that runs while your laptop is closed.
Let's begin!
What Grok Bot is
The one-line version is that a Bot is a named teammate you message, and the actual computing happens one layer below it.
The word "bot" suggests a separate program running somewhere. It is closer to a saved role with its own memory, sitting on a machine it shares with every other role you create.
A Bot is defined by three things you write:
A short name
One primary job
And a description of how it should work.
In exchange, you get a persistent conversation thread, and the Bot keeps working context across turns.
As per the official docs, a Bot retains stable working preferences, important facts, and summaries from its work. It does not replay every prior message.

The computer is the other half. Every Bot on your account uses one persistent cloud computer with a browser, a filesystem, and a terminal. It is assigned to your user account, not to any individual Bot.
Each Bot gets its own screen on that shared machine. Several Bots can therefore drive browser and desktop tools at the same time, though one Bot runs one computer-use task on its screen at a time
In the docs and in the app, a Bot means one persistent named agent. It is not a separate machine, a separate container, or a separate model instance.
As a useful analogy, you can relate it to an office setting.
The cloud computer is the office, and each Bot is a coworker with their own desk. There are different people, jobs, and notebooks, but one filing cabinet and one set of keys.
That analogy also explains the trade-off, which we will return to in detail. Shared keys make handoffs free. They also mean the roster shares one set of consequences.
In summary, a Bot is a role plus a memory plus a thread. The machine underneath is singular, persistent, and shared.
How it is built
Before the setup, let's look at how all the pieces fit together.
Specifically, there are five parts you should know about Grok Bot:
The persistent cloud computer
The computer runs in SpaceXAI's cloud, not on your Mac. So closing the app or the laptop does not stop a background turn or a scheduled routine.

There's a durability contract, which means that there is a shared workspace at /workspace, and files, browser state, and supported sign-ins are designed to survive normal computer updates and recovery.

Everything else is explicitly replaceable. Temporary directories, manually installed packages, and uncommitted application state carry no guarantee. Durable project files belong in the shared workspace.

SpaceXAI has not published the operating system, the image contents, or the machine specification. One widely shared report from a user who inspected the environment describes Debian with roughly eight virtual CPUs, around sixteen gigabytes of memory, and a disk in the hundred-gigabyte range, with no GPU.
The sharing model
As mentioned above, every Bot on your account uses the same computer, and the docs enumerate exactly what that means.
Browser cookies and signed-in sessions are shared. Files are visible to every Bot. Command-line credentials are shared. One Bot can continue from work another Bot saved.
This means that a research Bot can save a file, and a writing Bot picks it up with no upload or additional login. The handoff costs nothing because nothing has to be re-established.
Under this shared setting, you should not place a credential or a file on the computer if another Bot on your account should not use it.
The action layer
Grok Bot has two ways to interact with a service.
A connector gives a Bot a structured path into a supported service. Connectors appear as Plugins in the current app, and they are account-wide rather than per Bot.
The browser handles everything else like vendor portals, ad managers, older internal tools, anything without a clean programmatic interface.
Ideally, prefer a connector when one is available, because it is often more reliable than clicking through a website.
Since programmatic coverage of business software can be limited, it falls back to pixel-level control, which also means that it inherits every fragility of the underlying site.
So a layout change, a new consent prompt, or a session timeout can break a workflow that ran fine earlier.
Authentication and the takeover flow
Sessions persist on the shared browser, so you usually do not sign in again for each task. Signing in once for one Bot makes that session available to your other Bots.
For anything sensitive, the Bot hands you the machine, like in case of passwords, passkeys, two-factor codes, CAPTCHAs, payment or identity checks, and sites that explicitly require a human.
Practically, you open the Agent Computer, take control, complete only the blocked step, return control, and tell the Bot to continue.
For supported connections, there is a secure secret request instead. The value is masked, excluded from the transcript, and not shown to the model.
Never paste a password or a one-time code into ordinary chat. The takeover flow exists precisely so those values stay out of the transcript.
Agent Memory
Memory is maintained per Bot.
Duplicating a Bot copies its profile, settings, enabled skills, routines, and avatar, but not its conversation history or learned memory.
The mechanism behind that memory is not published. Whether it is a summary buffer, a file on disk, a retrieval index, or some combination is not stated anywhere in the documentation.
In summary, the engineering story is one durable machine, a connector-first action layer with a browser fallback, human-in-the-loop authentication, and per-Bot memory whose internals stay private.
Bots, skills, and routines
Just like with any other agent, you should run one real task first. Then correct the output until it is reliable. Once you are satisfied, save the method as a skill.
This video depicts that process:
Once you are satisfied, only then turn it into a routine.
Creating a Bot properly
Press Cmd and N or click on the "+" icon, choose Create new agent, then open Bot actions and Edit Profile to set the name, title, description, and avatar.
You can also chat with the bot and describe what you need to fill this info:
The description holds rules that should stay true, and the conversation holds task-specific instructions.
A description like "never send external messages without approval" belongs in the profile. "Draft follow-ups for these twelve accounts" belongs in the thread.
Like any other Agent, specific jobs beat general ones.
For instance, Talent Scout and Expense Manager give the Bot something to build context around. General Helper gives it almost nothing, and its saved context becomes hard to reuse.
An account can hold up to 50 Bots and group chats combined. Start with the smallest useful roster and add a Bot only when a job has a stable specialist role.
Skills
A skill is a reusable set of instructions for how to do a task. It captures the steps, the decision rules, the expected output, and the safety boundaries.
Skills are available across your Bots, though a Bot may still need the relevant connector or login to use one.
You reference a saved skill by typing a forward slash (/) in the composer, and you mention Bots, groups, routines, and connectors with the at sign.
An ideal skill should mention six things:
When to use it
The required inputs and access
The sequence of work
How to validate the result
What to return
And what requires approval.
Teaching a skill by demonstration
When the Teach a task control is available, you can show a browser workflow instead of describing it.
Open a one-to-one conversation and its computer view, choose Teach a task, describe the result, perform the workflow once, then stop the recording.
The video below depicts this in action:
Teaching records visible computer interaction for up to ten minutes. Do note that it does not record microphone audio.
Recording lowers the barrier for people who would never write a procedure by hand. It also moves the work of hardening that procedure onto the human.
Important: Re-test a demonstrated skill after any website, connector, or source format change. A workflow learned from one pass through a site has no defence against that site changing.
Routines
A routine assigns a workflow to one Bot and tells it when to run. Schedules are the common case, and event triggers are supported where the underlying integration exists.
You can create one by asking the owning Bot in plain language.
A good request names the schedule and time zone, the input source, the expected result, the approval boundary, and what should happen when a source is missing.
Event triggers come through Cursor account integrations, such as a Slack message or a GitHub notification. These are separate from the Slack and GitHub plugins and may need their own connection flow.
Use a test run before enabling anything. A test run performs real work, so keep the inputs safe and write actions behind approval.
A Bot can own up to 50 routines, and the app keeps the 20 most recent run records for each. Deleting a routine is permanent and does not support undo.
In summary, skills describe how, routines decide when, and the gap between a working task and a safe automation is filled by you.
Working with more than one Bot
One Bot is useful. But ideally, the reason to add a second is to have another stable specialist role.
Group chats hold two to six Bots and exist for handoffs that need to be visible. You select the Bots, describe the shared outcome, and say who owns the next step.
You can interact normally, and the participating Bots decide who answers.
Alternatively, you can use the "at" sign when one teammate owns the request, and reserve the everyone mention for genuine group updates.
Bots also message each other asynchronously outside groups. The receiving Bot wakes, handles the request, and replies later, and the handoff stays visible in the conversation.
One current limit is that Bot-to-group handoff messages are text-only, so a Bot that needs another to inspect an image should send it directly.
Ideally ask for a single bot at each stage. Too many parallel handoffs create duplicate work and noisy updates, which is the failure mode that shows up once a roster grows past four or five Bots.
A direct message from you outranks background work and can redirect the current turn.
Auto review
Where enforcement is available, Grok Bot evaluates tool calls and computer actions before they run.
Require Approval rules always stop matching actions.
Always Allow rules let matching actions proceed only when the automated review finds no other reason to stop.
When both match, Require Approval wins.
Two important caveats to note:
Auto Review is model-based, so the docs position it as a complement to least privilege rather than a replacement.
Personal rules are stored on the current desktop and synced to its computer, which means a second installation needs its own check.
What happens to your local machine
By this point, it should be clear that the cloud computer and your Mac are different things.
A Bot only runs commands locally when that capability is enabled, and you approve it.
The setting is available under Settings, then General, then Agent, then Execution on Local Computer.
Set local execution to never allowed unless a Bot has a specific reason to work on your local files. This does not restrict the cloud computer in any way.
Grok Bot vs. Hermes Agent
Both give an agent a persistent computer. That is where the similarity stops.

Hermes is open source and self-hosted. You bring the machine, whether that is a Mac Mini at home or a virtual private server, and you run the agent on it. Grok Bot is a managed product where the machine is provisioned for you, and you never see it.
The difference shows up most sharply in memory and skills.

Hermes exposes both as files you can read and edit. Identity lives in SOUL.md, facts live in MEMORY.md and USER.md with hard character limits, sessions are searchable in SQLite, and skills are Markdown files with structured frontmatter that the agent writes and revises itself.
Grok Bot exposes none of that. Memory is described by behaviour rather than by format, and a skill is something you inspect through the interface rather than a file you open.

Hermes also ships maintenance machinery that Grok Bot has no equivalent for. The Curator prunes and archives unused agent-written skills in the background, and the companion GEPA pipeline evolves skills offline against execution traces rather than asking the agent to grade itself.

Grok Bot's advantage runs the other direction. Multi-agent coordination is a first-class product surface rather than something you assemble. Group chats, asynchronous handoffs, ownership passing, and a shared browser session across the roster all work without configuration.

The choice is mostly about who absorbs the operations. Hermes gives you inspectable files and real isolation, and asks you to run and maintain the machine. Grok Bot removes the maintenance and takes the isolation away with it.

The broader landscape follows the same axis. ChatGPT Work and Claude's computer use both operate software, but neither keeps a durable machine with persistent logins in the same way. Devin and Manus give a sandbox per task or project, which is exactly the model Grok Bot moved away from.
Setting it up on macOS
The whole setup runs in a few minutes.
All the instructions are specified here: https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/get-started.
Essentially, open the Grok Bot access page and choose the matching download.
Open the disk image, drag Grok Bot to Applications, and launch it. Confirm with Open if macOS asks.
Choose Get started on the welcome screen, finish authentication in the browser window that opens, and return to the app. Organizations on single sign-on complete their usual flow here.
Onboarding then introduces Bots, the shared computer, and routines, and asks which tools you use. Answering shapes the first teammate suggestions and does not connect or modify anything by itself.
Your cloud computer provisions in the background while that runs, and the last step opens Meet a future teammate.
Next, pick a suggested teammate or choose Create your own, then give it a short name, one primary job, and a description of how it should work.
A strong first request has five parts
The outcome you want finished
The important sources
The constraints on what it must avoid or ask about
The deliverable
And the point where it should stop for you.
Start with something that needs no login at all, like attaching a document and asking for a structured summary with citations gives a result in about five minutes and confirms the machine is healthy.

When a Bot reaches a service that needs authentication, it hands you the computer. Open Agent Computer from the conversation, take control, enter the password or passkey or two-factor code, then return control.
The session persists on the shared computer afterwards. Every other Bot on your account can now use it, which is the moment the shared boundary becomes concrete rather than theoretical.
For supported services, install a connector from Settings and then Plugins instead. It is the more reliable path where one exists.
Finally, once a result is repeatable, ask the Bot to save the method as a named skill. Include the source systems, the output format, and the rules about what requires approval.
Only after that should you create a routine.
As a takeaway, resist automating on the first good output. The documented order exists because a routine inherits every unstated assumption in the task it was built from.
Wrapping up
The design decision underneath Grok Bot is small to state and large in consequence. State moved out of the context window and into a machine that stays running.
That way, a handoff between two Bots costs nothing, and what lets a routine fire at eight in the morning with your laptop shut.
It is also why the documentation tells you not to treat separate Bots as a security boundary, because free handoffs and shared credentials are the same fact seen from two sides.

The practical path through it is the one the docs prescribe and most people skip. One narrow Bot, one real task, corrections until the output is reviewable, then a skill, then a routine, with anything consequential behind approval.

Compared to Hermes, you are trading inspectable files and genuine isolation for a machine you do not have to run. Which side of that trade is right depends entirely on what you are willing to sign into a computer you cannot see.
I will keep writing about Grok Bot as the beta develops, particularly once enterprise controls and any per-Bot isolation land.
👉 Over to you. What is the first role you would hand to a Bot?
That's a wrap!
